a.strongest_frame: s4 infrared-view (24.2 to 26.4 s). The drone holds at the point-of-interest ring and the illustrated infrared view opens out of its lens along dashed sight lines. The inset is labelled 'Illustrative infrared view' and the IrView shimmer is a function of the film clock. This is the clearest input-to-evidence relation in the film. Runner-up is s1 station-wide (0 to 3.08 s): the hood finishes opening, the rotors spin up and the drone lifts out of the bay over a caliche pad with a pumpjack. That gives a real action in the first second, with the first reward at 0.546 s.
a.weakest_frame: s5 review-wide (28.75 to 31.09 s), the film's declared signature shot and performed turn. A paper seal reading 'Certified inspector' scales down from 1.4x and fades onto the survey footage by itself, and a dashed outline draws itself round the shimmer. No person, hand, stylus or cursor exists anywhere in the film. With labels covered, the software appears to certify the leak.

blocking_defects.failed_criterion: quality_contract.dominant_action and contact_and_consequence. Storyboard-critic brief: 'A person must perform the claimed action'. MODERN_FILM narration-picture: 'A topic match, caption or label cannot replace a pictured causal step'.
blocking_defects.defect: The certified inspector's review is the story's turn (cinematic_contract.turn_scene s5, art_direction.signature_shot s5-event-2, clauses n5a and n5b 'Then a certified inspector reviews the footage to identify any emissions'), but nobody performs it. In LeakReviewSupport.ReviewScreen/InspectorMark, the mark's scale runs from 1+0.4*(1-smooth(mark)) and its opacity from clamp(mark*2.5), so a seal reading 'Certified inspector' zooms and fades onto the footage on its own. DrawnDashes then draws the outline round the shimmer by itself, and in LeakReviewFilm.followUp the 'Follow-up inspection' tag flies along a Bezier curve from the screen into a valve vignette with no hand or carrier. The support module's header confirms 'no ... person: the inspector appears only as a mark and a line'. The only proof of who acts is printed text. The mark uses the same self-animating UI grammar and the same amber accent (the InspectorMark check stroke is LR.amber) as the software's 'Anomaly' flag in s2 and the amber point-of-interest ring in s4. With labels covered, a viewer sees the software flag the valve, the drone confirm it and the system stamp it, which inverts the answer the film exists to give. The source permits a generic human: c7 (a certified OGI inspector reviews the survey footage) and c15 (an emission visually confirmed by a certified OGI inspector). Earlier registered Claude-lane episodes show this engine can perform it: clinic-answer-v1 uses anonymous hands, and flood-station-v1 has an articulated seated responder and a technician. Required correction: author a generic, unnamed, disclosed certified inspector at the review screen. Show at least shoulder to hand, oriented toward the footage. That person's own stylus or scrub action must draw the outline round the shimmer and press the confirmation, and the follow-up must leave through a visible handoff that person makes. Give the human confirmation a colour and shape grammar distinct from the AI amber.

blocking_defects.failed_criterion: quality_contract.closing_payoff and dominant_action. Captions and labels can't supply a missing principal action.
blocking_defects.defect: The close repeats the s5 construction. s9-event-1 re-presses the same self-drawing InspectorMark (press = sin(pi*r/0.3)*0.06) and draws an amber check stroke with no actor. s9-event-2 then draws a dashed box labelled 'AI' that stays empty. The opening question asks 'who decides', and the closing image answers it only with the printed words 'Certified inspector' on a badge. That mark is indistinguishable in kind from the software's s2 flag, so the closing image doesn't show a person deciding (n8a 'a certified inspector confirms the leak'). Required correction: carry the s5 inspector into the close. The person confirms beside the empty AI box, and the station in the window may stay as the bookend.

blocking_defects.failed_criterion: quality_contract.continuity and the story_contract source_limit ('the letter doesn't say what the AI adds'). news-reporting.md: 'An outline or highlight identifies a region; it does not prove that a machine detected, measured or classified it.'
blocking_defects.defect: The companies' AI alert claim is drawn on the very valve that later leaks. FlightScreen's own doc says 'the anomaly marker sits on the point of interest valve'. The flag rises at route[1] over a valve symbol, and that valve is the s4 point-of-interest ring (lit amber on arrival), the s4/s5 infrared shimmer, the inspector's outline and the follow-up tag's destination. The film therefore asserts visually that the AI flagged this leak and the inspector then confirmed it. c4 is a companies' claim about alerts for 'anomalies to normal operations'. Its scope note says it does not mention methane and the EPA letter doesn't describe it. c8 and the closing line say the letter doesn't say what the AI adds. The picture invents a specific AI contribution, the leak location, and contradicts the film's own empty AI box. The attribution tag 'The companies say' labels the claim but does not undo the invented causal link. Required correction: show the claimed alert as a generic operations anomaly that is not placed on the methane point of interest or emission chain, and keep the attribution tag. Stop sharing the AI-alert amber with the point-of-interest arrival and the inspector's confirmation.

story_review.one_viewing_summary: The intended chain, reconstructed from the executable code: A generic drone lifts from a hooded station on a caliche Permian pad and flies out while a Texas card pins the Permian and Austin. A desk tablet's flight screen raises an amber 'Anomaly' flag on a valve, and a paper tag reading 'The companies say' hooks onto it. An unsealed approval letter takes a crooked 'September 30th, 2025' stamp and an 'Approved' mark beside 'Periodic methane screening'. The drone flies a dashed route to a ring over that valve and an illustrative infrared view of the valve's warm shimmer opens. On a review screen a 'Certified inspector' seal lands on the footage, rings the shimmer and sends a 'Follow-up inspection' tag to the valve. A long letter scrolls to its protocol title, where AI is highlighted once. A separate leak-reporting program tag gets a 'Delayed' bar beside January 22nd, 2027, then an October 7th card and a 'Will propose to rescind' tag. Finally the seal draws a check beside an empty AI box while the station closes outside the window.
story_review.opening_to_ending: The film opens on a machine acting alone (the drone leaving its station) under the question of who decides a leak is real. It ends on a badge check and an empty AI box. Because no person ever acts and the AI flag sits on the same valve the badge confirms, the ending's answer, a person and not the software, survives only in printed words. The bookend station in the window closes the loop visually, but the answer itself is not pictured.
story_review.weakest_transition: s4 to s5 (26.4 s). The infrared footage slides onto the review panel, but the reviewer never enters. The handoff from machine sensing to human judgment, the one the whole film turns on, is carried by an object that applies itself. The secondary weak point is s6 to s7 (38.72 s), the detour into a separate program.

consolidated_correction: 1. Human turn (s5, and carried into s9): add a generic, unnamed, disclosed certified inspector at the review screen, visible from shoulder to hand and facing the footage. That person's own stylus or scrub action draws the outline on the shimmer and confirms, and dispatches the follow-up through a visible handoff. Give human confirmation its own colour and shape grammar, separate from the AI amber. The engine has precedent for this (clinic-answer-v1 hands, flood-station-v1 articulated responder and technician).

2. AI claim (s2): move the companies' 'Anomaly' alert off the methane point-of-interest valve and the emission chain. Keep 'The companies say'. Stop reusing the alert amber for point-of-interest arrival and inspector confirmation.

3. Example identity (s1, s3 to s4, s9): disclose on screen when the film moves from the Chevron pilot (DroneLife) to the EPA-described approved method, or restage so the review room and closing window do not return to the s1 pilot pad. If the s1 station stays, bind the DroneLife drone-in-a-box and base-station sentence as a claim.
4. Disclosures: keep 'Illustration. A separate program, no drone' through s8, and make every chip state what is actually illustrated.
5. Authored-art bindings: make each action_uses view match the shot that performs its event in each treatment (A: s4 flight in poi-close, s5 review-panel, s7 program-calendar; B: s1 station-wide).

6. Treatment B: rebuild it as a genuinely different complete treatment that executes its decision-first angle, or replace it, and bring wall views to 40 percent or less with the region behind the opening.

These corrections reuse the existing two authored groups and the unchanged script and claims (the claim addition in item 3 needs validator binding). They add no third treatment or reviewer.
